title: From syllables to words

bigIdea.text: Every Arabic word is a chain of syllables. A syllable starts with a letter and its vowel; it can end there, stretch, or close on a sukun. Read the chain one link at a time, then smoothly.

proper.text: Three building blocks: an open short syllable (letter + short vowel: بَ 'ba'), an open long syllable (letter + long vowel: بَا 'baa', 2 counts) and a closed syllable (letter + vowel + a sakin letter: بَبْ 'bab').
A shadda splits across two syllables: its first copy closes one syllable and its second opens the next (ـبَّـ = 'b | ba').

A syllable always starts with a consonant (hamza counts as one), never with a vowel alone or with a sakin letter. That is why a word starting with ٱ needs its joining vowel when you start on it, or a link from the word before.
Method for a new word: split it into syllables with your finger, say each one slowly, say them again joined at an even pace, then check against Sheikh al-Minshawi.
In 112:3 every word ends in a closed syllable; in 113:2 the last word is three open short syllables.

provenance.source: Tanzil text 112:3 (each word ends with sukun) and 113:2 word 3 (three letters, each with fatha)

extras.text: Reading syllable by syllable is a stage, not the goal. As your eyes learn common words, you will read them whole; keep splitting only the new or difficult ones.

note.text: Every word ends in a closed syllable (a letter with sukun).
Three syllables: two closed by a sukun, then an open one.
Three open short syllables: each letter has a fatha.
The shadda on ي splits across two syllables, then comes a long alif.
Starting on this word: four syllables, closed, closed, long, then open short.

drills.prompt: Open, long, closed: بَ · بَا · بَبْ, then تِ · تِي · تِبْ
Build a chain: بَ + تَبْ, first slowly as two syllables, then smoothly as one word (ba-tab).

questions.q: Which of these is a CLOSED syllable?
explain: Right: it ends on a sakin letter.

questions.q: Which of these is an open LONG syllable?
explain: A shadda alone is not a syllable; it splits across two.

questions.q: How does a shadda affect syllables?
options: Its first copy closes one syllable and its second opens the next
explain: Length comes from madd letters, not from shadda.
It adds a consonant; nothing is removed.

questions.q: Why does a word starting with ٱ need a vowel when you start on it?
options: A syllable can't start with a sakin letter, so the joining hamza and its vowel are said
To mark the end of the word
explain: ٱ is not a madd letter.
It is said when you start on it.
It is at the start of the word.

questions.q: What is the best order for reading a new word?
options: Split into syllables, say each slowly, then join them evenly
Read it as fast as you can first
explain: Arabic is read right to left.

questions.q: How many counts does the vowel of an open long syllable last?
explain: One count is a short vowel.
Four counts is a longer madd (Stage 2).
It is a vowel, so it has length.

questions.q: How many syllables are in بَتَبْ (ba-tab)?
explain: There are two vowels, so at least two syllables.
The final sakin ب closes 'tab'; it is not a syllable on its own.
That counts letters and marks, not syllables.
Arabic syllables never start with a bare vowel.
A sakin letter closes a syllable; it can't open one.
A shadda is split across two syllables.

questions.q: Which sign tells you a syllable is closed?
options: A sukun on its last letter
explain: A madd letter makes it long, not closed.

questions.q: After splitting a word, how should the joined reading sound?
options: Even, with no stops between the syllables
With a pause after every syllable
With every syllable stretched to 2 counts
explain: Pauses inside a word break it apart.

questions.q: In a chain, a long vowel (ا و ي after its matching vowel) makes its syllable…
explain: A sukun closes a syllable; a madd letter lengthens it.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a syllable type in Quran reading?
options: A syllable that starts with a vowel alone
explain: Right: every syllable starts with a consonant.

questions.q: Your reading of a word doesn't match Sheikh al-Minshawi. What do you do?
options: Split it again and check each syllable's vowel and length

remnote: Three syllable types == Open short (بَ), open long (بَا, 2 counts), closed (بَبْ)
Shadda in syllables == First copy closes one syllable, second opens the next
Reading a new word == Split, say each syllable, join evenly, check with Minshawi
taskNow: Read 112:3 syllable by syllable, then smoothly, five times; record the fifth time, then press Play mine (step 5, Practise) and compare it with the reference.
